keyVerseText: And they turned and went up by the way of Bashan: and Og the king of Bashan went out against them, he, and all his people, to the battle at Edrei.
rootMeaning: The root of עוֹג (ʻÔwg) is likely connected to the Hebrew root עוּג (ʻûwg), which means 'to bake,' specifically referring to baking round cakes. This etymology suggests a notion of roundness or circular form, which aligns with the lexicon's mention of עוֹג meaning 'long-necked,' possibly alluding to a physical characteristic. This root sense adds a tangible, physical dimension to the name beyond its function as a proper noun, emphasizing a distinctive feature that may have symbolized strength or stature.
usageInScripture: The word עוֹג appears 22 times in Scripture, predominantly as a proper name referring to Og, the Amorite king of Bashan. The translations consistently identify the name Og, often in conjunction with the land of Bashan or its king, revealing a consistent use as a title or identifier rather than a common noun. The variations in translation, such as 'of Og,' 'and Og,' or 'For only Og,' reflect its role in narrative and genealogical contexts, emphasizing Og's prominence as a historical and symbolic figure within the biblical text.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עוֹג as the name of a giant king who was one of the last of the Rephaim giants highlights the biblical theme of God's sovereignty over formidable earthly powers. Og's identity as a 'long-necked' or physically imposing figure underscores the reality of spiritual and physical opposition faced by God's people. Yet, the consistent biblical portrayal of Og's defeat serves as a reminder of God's faithfulness and power to deliver His people from seemingly insurmountable enemies. This reinforces the Christian faith's confidence in God's ultimate authority and protection, encouraging believers to trust in His providence amidst challenges.
keyVerseReflection: Numbers 21:33 recounts, 'And they turned and went up by the way of Bashan: and Og the king of Bashan went out against them, he, and all his people, to the battle at Edrei.' The use of עוֹג here identifies the formidable leader opposing Israel, emphasizing the tangible threat he posed. The name evokes the historical and theological weight of this encounter, reminding readers of God's power to overcome even the mightiest adversaries on behalf of His people.
